text.p: Bre-X Minerals Ltd. completed its journey from rags to riches back to rags Tuesday as investors reduced the once C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) company to penny stock status.

Investors savaged the stock when it resumed trading for the first time since a report late on Sunday said the company's celebrated Busang gold find in Indonesia was basically worthless and that samples had been doctored.

Toronto Stock Exchange President Rowland Fleming said the affair highlighted the need for regulatory reform in Canada. But he defended the exchange's role in the Bre-X affair, saying the company easily met listing requirements.
Investors wiped out C$690 million ($501 million) of Bre-X's already reduced market value and the company was worth only about C$17 million ($12 million) at Tuesday's close.

The stock fell C$3.145 ($2.28) to C8.5 cents (6 cents) in active trading of 58.3 million shares. The volume set a record for a single stock on the exchange, topping the old mark of 38.5 million shares set by Black Swan Gold Mines Ltd. on April 16, 1996.
"It's shell company value, as they say. It's worthless," said John Ing, president of brokerage Maison Placements Canada, referring to Bre-X.
Discount brokers said they were receiving requests for Bre-X stock certificates from souvenir seekers.

Bre-X's Busang discovery, once thought to be the richest find of the century, was falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining," according to a report issued on Sunday by an independent consultant.

In late March, after prospective joint venture partner Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. issued a report saying it found insignificant gold at the Busang property in tests, Bre-X stock fell 80 percent, wiping C$3 billion ($2.2 billion) from the company's value.

Nasdaq did not resume trading the stock Tuesday, saying it was under "no obligation to trade companies that have admitted to fraudulent claims." The exchange said it called company officials to a May 13 hearing.
Despite the Nasdaq halt, some unauthorised trading occurred when the market opened, said Nasdaq spokesman Reid Walker. "So all of those trades have been cancelled."
Trading on Nasdaq will remain suspended until a decision on delisting the stock is made after the hearing, he said.

The TSE's Fleming said there were 12 provincial securities commissions in Canada but they did not function as well as centralized regulators in the United States, Britain, Germany and Japan, among others.
"No exchange may be able to stop the next Bre-X from happening," Fleming said in a speech prepared for a business group.

"But I would argue that a single securities commission can certainly make that possibility much more remote -- just as it did in Australia in the wake of a nickel scandal similar to Bre-X in the 1980s -- and a single commission can react much more quickly when a scandal of this proportion occurs."

The exchange's computers, seriously snarled by enormous Bre-X volume when the company's fairy tale began turning into a horror story in March, again choked on the heavy volume on Tuesday -- which topped 35 million shares in the first hour.
